text: The Jeffersons is an American sitcom created by Norman Lear that aired on CBS from January 18, 1975, to July 2, 1985, spanning eleven seasons and 253 episodes. Starring Isabel Sanford as Louise Jefferson and Sherman Hemsley as George Jefferson, the show follows a prosperous African-American couple who move from Queens to a high-rise apartment in Manhattan, New York City, due to the success of George's dry-cleaning chain, Jefferson Cleaners. It is a spin-off of All in the Family, where the Jeffersons were neighbors of the Bunkers; George's character was specifically created for Hemsley, who was initially unavailable due to starring in the Broadway musical Purlie, leading Lear to introduce Henry Jefferson, played by Mel Stewart, as George's younger brother until Purlie ended. The Jeffersons premiered the week after the All in the Family episode "The Jeffersons Move Up," which aired on January 11, 1975, and featured Louise, her son Lionel (played by Mike Evans), and George moving into the Colby East high-rise. The show's concept was inspired by feedback from Black Panthers who criticized the portrayal of Black people on television, prompting Lear to develop a series highlighting upward mobility. The series evolved into a traditional sitcom but occasionally addressed serious issues such as alcoholism, racism, suicide, gun control, transgender identity, the KKK, and adult illiteracy, with the epithets "nigger" and "honky" used occasionally, especially in early seasons. The show had one spin-off, Checking In, centered on Florence Johnston (Marla Gibbs), who becomes a hotel cleaning manager, lasting only four episodes before returning to The Jeffersons with the story that the hotel burned down. The Jeffersons shared continuity with E/R, featuring Lynne Moody in a guest role, and Sherman Hemsley guest-starred as George in two episodes of a one-season series. The show ended controversially when CBS canceled it without a proper finale, announcing the cancellation at the upfront presentation the day before the final episode aired on July 2, 1985, nearly two months prior; cast members learned through newspapers, tabloids, or Entertainment Tonight. Isabel Sanford criticized the cancellation as disrespectful. The cast later reunited in a stage play, "The Jeffersons Live: The Movin' On Up Tour," and made guest appearances in later series, including The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air (1995 and 1996) and Tyler Perry's House of Payne (2011). In 1985, Hemsley and Sanford made a joint guest appearance in the Italian comedy Grand Hotel, with their voices dubbed by Enzo Garinei and Isa di Marzio. As of 2023, surviving main cast members include Marla Gibbs, Berlinda Tolbert, Damon Evans, and Jay Hammer. The Jeffersons' theme song, "Movin' On Up," was co-written by Ja'Net DuBois and Jeff Barry, inspired by DuBois's dream of providing her mother with a comfortable retirement. The show changed time slots at least 15 times during its run, most commonly airing on Sunday nights. It initially ranked fourth in its first season, later entering the Top 30, peaking at No. 3 in 1982, and remaining in the Top 20 for several seasons. The series was rebroadcast on CBS from February 4, 1980, to September 25, 1981, and released on DVD by Sony Pictures Home Entertainment from 2002 to 2007, later acquired by Mill Creek and Shout! Factory, with the complete series released in a 33-disc collection in 2014. The Jeffersons earned 14 Emmy nominations, winning two: Marla Gibbs won Best Supporting Actress in a Comedy Series from 1981 to 1985, Sherman Hemsley received a nomination in 1984, and Larry M. Harris won Outstanding Video Tape Editing in 1983; Isabel Sanford was nominated for seven consecutive Best Actress Emmys from 1979 to 1985, winning in 1981, making her the first African-American actress to win that award. The show received five Golden Globe nominations. Critics have criticized it as stereotypical, with Gregory Kane calling it demeaning in 1999. The series had many two-part episodes and was known for its recurring characters, including Tom and Helen Willis (played by Franklin Cover and Roxie Roker), who were an interracial couple; Allan (Jay Hammer) and Jenny (Berlinda Tolbert), who married in 1976 and had a daughter, Jessica; and Paul Benedict as Harry Bentley, a British neighbor with a bad back and a habit of being slammed in the door. Ned Wertimer played Ralph Hart, the tip-hungry doorman, and Danny Wells portrayed Charlie, the bar owner and alcoholic, whose drinking issue was addressed in a season 11 episode. Mike Evans (Lionel) left after the first season, with Damon Evans (no relation) taking over until halfway through season 4, and Evans made his final appearance in "Lionel Gets the Business." Mike Evans and Tolbert returned in 1979–1980, with Tolbert's character pregnant, and Evans appeared in only one more season. The series' eighth season reached No. 3, becoming the first African-American sitcom in years to peak in the top 5. Paul Benedict left for a season and a half in 1981, returning in the final two seasons. The show's ratings declined after 1980, and it ended with the episode "Red Robins" on July 2, 1985. On May 22, 2019, ABC aired a live stage production of Norman Lear's All in the Family and The Jeffersons, featuring Marla Gibbs as Florence Johnston.

The stage show featured recreations of the episodes "A Whole Lot of Trouble," "Social Insecurity," and "My Wife... I Think I'll Keep Her." The tour started in Detroit, Michigan, with a six-city run, and although Roker dropped out, Berlinda Tolbert (who played Jenny) and Ned Wertimer (who played Ralph) returned to reprise their roles for the Los Angeles performance in 1994. On May 22, 2019, ABC aired Live in Front of a Studio Audience: Norman Lear's All in the Family and The Jeffersons, produced by Norman Lear and Jimmy Kimmel, starring Woody Harrelson, Marisa Tomei, Jamie Foxx, Wanda Sykes, Ike Barinholtz, Kerry Washington, and Ellie Kemper, with Marla Gibbs reprising her role as Florence Johnston.
